blindSummary:
This country is one of the world's most severe environments for trans people — but with a unique bifurcation. Same-sex conduct carries the death penalty, and a trans woman was raped in intelligence-ministry custody (a documented 2023 case at the capital's main prison). The capital's city council ordered trans people to avoid "busy" areas of the city. Trans people who have not had surgery face immorality and indecency provisions (imprisonment, fines, lashes) and documented forced-transition pressure — an exiled LGBTIQ+ organisation describes four decades of forcing gay people to choose between transitioning and death.

However, transsexuality IS legally recognised here (under a 1987 religious edict by the state's founding senior cleric), and gender-affirming surgery is state-funded — making this one of the few countries in the region with any legal recognition of trans identity, and a trans medical-tourism hub. A post-operative trans visitor with matching documents is in a structurally different and better position than a pre-operative or non-binary visitor, or anyone perceived as same-sex-active — who face the death penalty, state-custody sexual violence, and forced-transition coercion.
blindOutOfScope: General state-surveillance risks, a compulsory religious dress code for all women, and the risk of arbitrary detention for foreign nationals affect all travellers; only trans-specific risk is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: International broadcaster (March 2024): the capital's city council spokesman said transgender people should congregate only in certain parts of the city and avoid 'busy' areas - official guidance highlighting how the LGBT community is shunned; most LGBT people here hide their orientation and lead double lives for fear of persecution.

Exiled human-rights monitoring group (Aug 2026): a trans woman incarcerated in the capital's main prison recounts in a letter that after her May 2023 arrest she was taken blindfolded to an intelligence-ministry detention facility, searched, and raped by a masked man; officials promised release in exchange for silence and threatened her against speaking out.

Exiled LGBTIQ+ organisation submission (Feb 2025) to a UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, titled to the effect that the authorities see them as criminals and documenting the forces driving LGBTIQ+ displacement: survey of 25 LGBTIQ+ people who fled this country (96% from ethnic minorities) documenting systematic persecution driving displacement.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations criminalised with a maximum penalty of death; trans people who have undergone surgery may change legal gender markers but face violence, discrimination and harassment; strict censorship bans LGBTIQ media; a UN fact-finding mission (March 2025) found discriminatory public statements by officials at the highest levels and that LGBTQ+ people arrested in the 2022 protests suffered 'dehumanising insults, threats and treatment amounting to torture'.

A foreign home ministry's country-of-origin assessment for asylum purposes on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v5.0, Dec 2025): the religious penal code criminalises all same-sex activity (flogging up to the death penalty); no discrimination protections; convictions on pretext of more severe charges; gender reassignment surgery is permitted and may be subsidised after a 'gender identity disorder' diagnosis, but is invasive and often sub-standard; recognition only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process; an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution.

LGBTQ news site (Oct 2025): trans medical tourism is booming in this country - the government promotes discounted gender-affirming surgery packages to foreigners to earn foreign currency, while the industry's expertise stems from decades of forcing gay people to choose between transitioning and death; also reports 100 trans inmates presumed dead after a cross-border military strike on one of the country's prisons.

Business daily (July 2024): this country's transgender policy might seem surprisingly liberal - the state pays for gender-transition surgery - but at the cost of personal dignity; profiles a trans citizen and examines the paradox of state-funded transition alongside criminalisation of homosexuality.

Exiled LGBTIQ+ organisation's submission to this country's UN periodic review (48th session, Jan-Feb 2025): human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people in this country - documentation of persecution, violence and legal discrimination.

International human-rights organisation report (Nov 2005): two further executions for consensual same-sex conduct under this country's penal code, part of the pattern of death-penalty application to LGBT people.
blindLocalsOnly: The 1987 religious edict's legal recognition of transsexuality and state-funded gender-affirming surgery are resident-facing; the forced-transition pressure on gay people is a resident phenomenon, though it signals the state's posture.
blindTangential: Same-sex conduct carries the death penalty — a catastrophic risk for any visitor perceived as same-sex-active, including trans people whose documents don't match their presentation or relationships.
